props.title: Father of the Bride
props.initialSlug: Overprotective dad faces daughter's wedding chaos

sections.content: **Father of the Bride** (1991) perfectly captures the emotional whirlwind of watching your child grow up through Steve Martin's pitch-perfect performance as George Banks. This remake of the 1950 Spencer Tracy classic modernizes the story while maintaining its heart. Director Charles Shyer crafts intimate family moments that feel genuine - from George's first reaction to the engagement to his supermarket meltdown over hot dog buns. The film sparked a wave of wedding-focused family comedies in the 1990s, including **My Best Friend's Wedding** (1997) and **The Wedding Singer** (1998).

sections.content: The film's success lies in its ability to balance comedy with genuine emotional depth. Martin Short's flamboyant wedding planner Franck Eggelhoffer provides the perfect comedic counterpoint to Martin's increasingly frazzled father. Their interactions, particularly during the wedding planning sequences, created a template for the "expensive wedding chaos" subplot that became a staple in films like **Monster-in-Law** (2005) and **Wedding Crashers** (2005).

What sets **Father of the Bride** (1991) apart is its focus on the father-daughter relationship rather than just the romance. While Annie's fiancé Brian is present, the story's emotional core is George's journey of learning to let go. This influenced later films like **Because I Said So** (2007) and **27 Dresses** (2008) that explored family dynamics within wedding narratives. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Family Comedy

sections.content: The early 1990s marked a shift toward more emotionally grounded family comedies. **Father of the Bride** (1991) arrived alongside films like **Parenthood** (1989) and **Mrs. Doubtfire** (1993) that moved beyond simple slapstick to explore complex family relationships. These films showed that comedy could tackle serious themes while remaining accessible and entertaining.
